subject: english
prompt: The unit opens by asking how 'words' can be 'carried'. In the main text, who is the **carrier of words**?

image.alt: A red post box with letters flying out towards faraway homes

options.text: A radio announcer who reads out the news
The camels that carry goods across the Thar
Khetaram, the Gramin Dak Sewak who carries mail to remote hamlets
The BSF jawans who guard the border

hint: Think of who hefts a mailbag onto his shoulders every day.
explanation: Letters are **words on paper**, so the person who delivers them carries words from one family to another. Khetaram, a **Gramin Dak Sewak (GDS)**, is the sole postman of the Somarad Branch Post Office and links remote desert hamlets with faraway families. The BSF gives him lifts and the camels rest in the shade, but neither carries the mail.

subject: english
prompt: Before the main text, the book has a short passage about a trip to the desert. It has six blanks. The sentences here are slightly reworded. Match each sentence with the word from the box that fills its blank.

image.alt: Camels resting in the little shade of a tree under a blazing desert sun

left.text: Our bodies sent warning ___ that a noon visit was a mad idea.
We had decided to visit the sand ___ in the afternoon.
We drove past a few small ___, each with only a handful of homes.
Not a single person was outdoors, ___ the blazing sun.
Even the camels were ___ in the little shade of the khejri trees.
The area was ___ of any network except BSNL.

hint: 'Devoid' is always followed by 'of'; tired, drooping animals are 'slumped'.
explanation: Our body sends **signals** (warnings); sand hills are **dunes**; small settlements are **hamlets**; nobody was out **defying** (standing up to) the sun; the camels were **slumped** (sitting heavily, drooping) in the shade; and the area was **devoid of** (lacking) other networks. The same words return in the main text: Khetaram's shoulder is *slumped* from years of carrying the mailbag, and he works *defying* the harsh desert.

subject: english

explanation: **Dhaanis** are small desert hamlets, clusters of a few homes, like the round huts at marker 6. topic: The long road to the border
prompt: The text tells us how far Khetaram's area is from certain places. Put the places in the order the mail passes them, from where it is **dispatched** to where it is **delivered**.

Jodhpur, about 330 km away
The point where the Barmer–Chohtan road crumbles into sand (10 km before)
The dhaanis near the Indo-Pakistan border
Barmer, the last railhead (120 km before)

hint: The farther a place is from the hamlets, the earlier the mail passes it.
explanation: Mail leaves **Jodhpur** (about 330 km away), reaches the last railhead at **Barmer** (120 km short of the hamlets), passes the **last phone** (50 km short), then the spot where the **Barmer–Chohtan road** crumbles into sand so soft that even bicycles can't **ply** (10 km short). From there only Khetaram's footprints carry it to the **dhaanis**, within 24 hours of dispatch.

subject: english
prompt: Select the **three** statements about Khetaram's work that are true according to the text.

Even a single delivery can mean covering 20 km.

Mail reaches the border within 24 hours of leaving Jodhpur.

explanation: Swirling **sandstorms** cover him in sand all day, turning him into a **walking sandman**. As water is too scarce for washing, he only wipes himself, and the sand that falls off makes a little 'dune' at his feet. The line is a vivid exaggeration that shows the harshness of his work, not a hobby or a chore.

subject: english
topic: British postal system and India Post
prompt: How was the purpose of India Post different from the purpose of the postal system the British set up in India?

image.alt: Two panels: mail moving only between a few office buildings, and mail fanning out to many village huts

options.text: The British system carried only parcels, while India Post carries only letters.
The British system reached every village, while India Post serves only cities.
The British system was free, while India Post charges for every letter.
The British system relayed company dak between administrative centres; India Post set out to bring the whole population within its reach.

hint: Look for the words 'mandate' and 'ambit'.
explanation: The British set up the system to **relay company dak between administrative centres**, that is, for running their administration. After independence, India Post's **mandate** was to bring the **entire population within the mailing ambit** (range). That is why post offices grew from **25,000 in 1947** to more than a lakh and a half today, and why GDS reach rural depositors.

subject: english
prompt: A postmaster explains that some special conditions help India Post keep a large number of GDS workers. Select the **three** conditions he mentions.

image.alt: A small village branch post office with a red letter box and a clock

They must have access to another means of livelihood.
They must retire on their 60th birthday.
They need to work only five hours a day.
They may continue to serve till the age of 65.

hint: One condition is about age, one about hours and one about another source of income.
explanation: The essential **criterion** for GDS selection is **access to another means of livelihood**; they work **only five hours a day** and may serve **after 60, till 65**. These conditions let India Post pay them a salary that gives an assured income. That is why Khetaram is grateful he can serve 'even after 60'. Nothing is said about owning a bicycle or a camel.

subject: english
topic: Extract: famine as a way of life
prompt: *“Akaal or famine is a way of life here. In a good year, I get one crop of bajra.”* Why does Khetaram call famine **'a way of life'**?

image.alt: A cracked, dry field with a single millet plant and an empty pot

options.text: Famine comes so often in this arid land that people have to live with it all the time.
People in the village celebrate famine as a festival.
He likes to fast because it keeps him fit for long walks.
The government declares a famine holiday every summer.

hint: 'A way of life' means something normal and constant.
explanation: In the **arid** (very dry) Thar, shortage of food and water is normal, so famine has become an ordinary part of life. Even in a **good year** (one with enough rain) he gets only **one crop of bajra**, which cannot feed his **family of five**; so he says they would starve without his job. Families here also depend partly on **money orders** sent by relatives.

prompt: A torn right corner tells the family that the letter brings news of a death, even before they open it. **Who most likely tore the corner?**

image.alt: A close-up of an envelope with its top right corner torn off

The sender of the letter
The receiver of the letter
The postmaster

explanation: The torn corner is a **sign** put on the envelope **before it is posted**, so it must be the **sender's** doing. Khetaram only notices it, and the receiver has not yet got the letter. That is why Khetaram knows the letter is **Ashubh Samachar** (bad news) and does not carry it into the house.

prompt: Put in order the steps Khetaram follows when he has a letter with news of a death.

image.alt: A closed doorway with scraps of torn paper fluttering away outside

He sees that the envelope's right corner is torn off.

Because **'Ashubh Samachar cannot be carried into the house'**, he **stands outside**, **reads the letter out twice** so that the family hears it clearly, then **tears it to bits**, muttering that 'bad news must be destroyed'. His actions match his beliefs exactly.

subject: english
prompt: Khetaram reads the sad letter twice at the door, then tears it up, saying *“Bad news must be destroyed.”* What does this **best** show about his nature?

He is afraid of reading letters in front of people.

explanation: He follows the village belief that bad news cannot be carried inside, and he reads the letter **twice** so that the grieving family understands it. This shows **respect for customs**, **sensitivity** and a **philosophical** nature. Reading it twice shows care, not haste or carelessness.

prompt: Khetaram is waiting for phone lines to reach his area. They are now only 50 km away. How might they change his job?

He would be moved to a city post office in Jodhpur.
He would only repair telephone lines instead of delivering mail.

hint: 'Dak' means post; 'sanchar' means communication.
explanation: When phone lines arrive, he might become a **Gramin Sanchar Sewak**, and his duty would **entail** (involve) carrying a **cell phone and the post** from home to home. So the job would grow; he would still deliver mail. He welcomes it, saying “**Main tayyar hoon**” (I'm ready).

subject: english
prompt: Khetaram says *“Main tayyar hoon”* (I'm ready) about his possible new role, then strides off with his sack to deliver mail before sundown. What does this show about him?

image.alt: A postman striding over the dunes with a sack on his shoulder as the sun goes down

options.text: He is tired of the job and is waiting to retire.
He wants a better-paid job in a city.
He is afraid that mobile phones will replace him.
He is eager to take on new duties and stays devoted to his work.

hint: 'Striding' means walking with long, confident steps.
explanation: Even after more than a decade and a half of hard work, he is **ready** to learn new things and take on more responsibility. **Striding** off to deliver Panna Devi's dak before sundown shows energy and **dedication**. Nothing in the text suggests he is tired, afraid or looking for a city job.

subject: english
prompt: People trust Gramin Dak Sewaks. Select the **three** examples from the text that show this.

image.alt: A letter that has been read, and a reply being written beside it

options.text: Villagers ask Khetaram to read their letters and draft replies.
Villagers insist on collecting their own mail from Jodhpur.
Rural depositors entrust their monthly savings to the post office in their area.
The BSF stopped giving him lifts once their camp arrived.
A plan to hand the GDS job to patwaris was rejected; villagers knew patwaris could not do it.

explanation: Everyone feels comfortable asking him to **read letters and draft replies**; **rural depositors entrust** their monthly savings to the post office; and the scheme to transfer the job to **patwaris** (village record keepers) was **summarily rejected**. Village elder Budh Singh says, “We knew they would not be able to do the job.” The BSF actually **always** gives him a lift, so the claim that it stopped is false, and villagers never fetch their own mail from Jodhpur.

prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

reason: The rules say that his load cannot be more than 28 kilos.

explanation: Both statements are true, but R does **not** explain A. The text says **severe heat** sometimes forces him to postpone deliveries till after sundown. The **28-kilo limit** on his load is a separate rule about the mailbag; it has nothing to do with the time of day he delivers.

prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

R is **true**: his appointment **more than a decade ago** gave him a **new lease of life** (a fresh chance to live well), since his bajra crop alone could not feed his family.

subject: english
prompt: The text ends: people like Khetaram are *“a part and parcel of our social fabric”*. What does the phrase **part and parcel** mean here?

image.alt: Colourful threads woven into a fabric, with letters and a home among them

options.text: an essential part that holds society together
people whose job is to deliver parcels and cloth
a small group that society could easily do without
people who make clothes for the village

hint: It is an idiom; don't read 'parcel' and 'fabric' literally.
explanation: **Part and parcel** is an idiom meaning an **essential, inseparable part** of something. **Social fabric** compares society to woven cloth: every thread matters. The author salutes people like Khetaram because they connect remote families, carry money and news, and are trusted by all; options about parcels and cloth take the words literally.

subject: english
prompt: Match each phrase from the unit with its meaning.

image.alt: A road that breaks up and disappears into desert sand, beside a thinning stream

left.text: crumbles into sand
give a new lease of life
turn into a trickle before drying out
bearing words across this desolate geography

right.text: get a chance to continue living
lessen gradually and then finally stop
carrying letters to less populated areas
fall asleep in the afternoon heat

hint: A 'trickle' is a very thin flow of water.
explanation: The road **crumbles into sand**: it breaks up and vanishes into the desert. Khetaram's job gave him **a new lease of life**, a fresh chance to live. A stream that **turns into a trickle before drying out** lessens gradually and then stops. **Bearing words across this desolate geography** means carrying letters across empty, thinly populated land. 'Fall asleep' fits none of them.

subject: english
prompt: These phrases come from the extract about Khetaram's khaki turban and the sandstorms. Tap the card with the **metaphor**.

image.alt: Five phrase cards from an extract, numbered 1 to 5

hint: A metaphor says something IS something else, without 'like' or 'as'.
explanation: Sandstorms turn him into **a walking sandman**: he is not literally made of sand, but the text calls him one to show how completely sand covers him. This direct comparison without 'like' or 'as' is a **metaphor**. 'Khetaram's khaki', 'scorching summer' and 'swirling sandstorms' are examples of **alliteration** (repeated first sounds).

subject: english
prompt: Select the **three** phrases from the same extract that are examples of **alliteration**.

image.alt: A figure in a khaki uniform and turban walking through a swirling sandstorm

options.text: scorching summer
turban and uniform
Khetaram's khaki
swirling sandstorms
the desert's furies

hint: Say each phrase aloud and listen for the same starting sound.
explanation: **Alliteration** is the repetition of the same first sound in words close together: the **k** sound in 'Khetaram's khaki', the **s** in 'scorching summer' and in 'swirling sandstorms'. 'Turban and uniform' has no repeated sound. 'The desert's furies' treats the weather as angry, so it is figurative, but it is not alliteration.

subject: english
prompt: All these sentences are in the **present perfect** (has/have + past participle). Match each one with what it expresses.

image.alt: A timeline arrow with an arc joining a past moment to now

left.text: Asha has just posted the letter.
Have you ever written a letter by hand?
Our village has grown into a small town over the years.
I have visited that post office many times.

right.text: an action repeated at different times
an action happening at this very moment

hint: Look at the signal words: just, ever, over the years, many times.
explanation: **Just** marks a **recently completed** action; **ever** asks about **life experience**; **has grown … over the years** shows **change over time**; **many times** shows an action **repeated at different times**. An action happening at this very moment needs the present continuous ('is posting'), not the present perfect.

subject: english
prompt: Tap the sentence that is in the **present perfect** tense.

image.alt: Five sentence cards about a postman, numbered 1 to 5

hint: Structure: has/have + third form of the verb.
explanation: **Has delivered** is **has + past participle**, so card 2 is in the present perfect: the action is complete and its result matters now. Card 1 is simple past ('delivered yesterday'), card 3 is past perfect (**had** delivered), card 4 is present continuous and card 5 is simple future.

subject: english
prompt: Choose the correct form: *“Riya ______ just ______ (receive) a parcel of old postcards from her grandmother, and she is opening it now.”*

image.alt: A parcel box opening with old postcards popping out

options.text: have … received
had … received
has … received
has … receive

hint: Singular subject; the result (the parcel) is here now.
explanation: The present perfect is **has/have + past participle**. 'Riya' is singular, so we use **has**, and the past participle of *receive* is **received**: *Riya has just received…* 'Have' does not agree with a singular subject, 'had received' (past perfect) clashes with 'is opening it now', and 'receive' is the base form, not the past participle.

subject: english
prompt: Tap the sentence that is in the **passive voice**.

image.alt: Five sentence cards about the post, numbered 1 to 5

hint: In the passive, the subject receives the action: a form of 'be' + past participle.
explanation: In **The letters are sorted at the post office**, the subject *letters* **receives** the action, and the verb is **are + sorted** (be + past participle), so it is passive. In all the other cards the subject does the action: villagers trust, the bus was carrying, the postman reads, the camels rested. 'Was carrying' is past continuous active, a common trap.

subject: english
prompt: Khetaram advises his nephew: *“Practise reading clearly as some of the villagers will expect you to read out the letters.”* Complete the passive version: *“Reading clearly should be practised, as you ______ to read out the letters by some of the villagers.”*

image.alt: A clipboard checklist with a shoe, a book, a pen and a shirt

options.text: will expect
will be expected
will be expect
are expecting

hint: Future passive: will + be + past participle.
explanation: 'The villagers **will expect** you' becomes 'you **will be expected** by the villagers': **will + be + past participle**, keeping the future tense. 'Will expect' and 'are expecting' are still active (and make no sense with 'by some of the villagers'), and 'will be expect' wrongly uses the base form instead of the past participle.

subject: english
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A person and a letter swapping places on either side of an arrow

assertion: 'A lot of stamina will be needed for this job' is in the passive voice.
reason: Every passive sentence must name the doer of the action with 'by'.
hint: Does the sentence say who will need the stamina?
explanation: A is **true**: *stamina* receives the action and the verb is **will be + needed**. R is **false**: the doer ('by + agent') is often **left out** when it is obvious or unimportant, as here. 'The mail is delivered **by the GDS**' names the doer, but many passives, like Khetaram's advice, do not.

subject: english
prompt: In the Speaking Activity, a postcard, an inland letter, an envelope and a money order form argue about who is most important. Which one could **best** argue for the point **'possibility of enclosures'**?

image.alt: Picture D

explanation: An **enclosure** is an extra item, such as a photo or a document, sent inside with a letter, and only an **envelope** can hold one. A **postcard** is an open card (cheap, but with little **privacy**), an **inland letter** is a single sheet folded and sealed with its own flaps, and a **money order form** is for sending money. subject: english
prompt: During the discussion, your friend says the postcard is the most useful item. You want to **disagree politely**. Which cue from the activity fits best?

image.alt: Two friends in a friendly discussion with speech bubbles

options.text: I totally agree that…

hint: Which cue first accepts the other view and then turns with 'but'?
explanation: **That's one way to look at it, but…** respects your friend's view and then introduces your own: polite disagreement. 'I totally agree' shows agreement, 'Some people say that…' reports others' views, and 'It seems to me that…' simply states your opinion without answering your friend's point.

subject: english
prompt: Arrange the parts of a **condolence message** in the correct order, as in Sawant Singh's message to his cousin.

image.alt: A softly glowing candle beside a white flower

items.text: Complimentary close (Yours sincerely,)
Date

Salutation (Dear …,)
Sender's name
Sorrow at the loss and condolences

explanation: A **condolence message** communicates sympathy to someone who has lost a loved one. It begins with the **date** and a **salutation**, then expresses **sorrow** and offers **condolences**, then **prays** for peace for the departed and strength for the family, and ends with a **complimentary close** and the **sender's name**. Keep it short, sincere and gentle.

prompt: The Writing Task asks for an essay on a quotation. Arrange the parts of the essay in the order given in the guidelines.

image.alt: Five stacked paragraph blocks of an essay and a pencil

items.text: Counterargument: a possible criticism of the quotation and why it is baseless
Introduction: the quotation, its speaker, why it appeals to you and the essay's purpose
Conclusion: a summary and a statement that leaves a lasting impression
Body paragraphs: a topic sentence, then evidence and examples, joined by transition words

hint: You answer criticism only after you have made your own points.
explanation: The guidelines give five paragraphs: **1 Introduction**, **2 and 3 Body**, **4 Counterargument**, **5 Conclusion**. Each body paragraph opens with a **topic sentence** and uses transition words such as 'For instance…', 'However…' and 'Consequently…'. The counterargument faces a possible criticism and shows why it is baseless, and the conclusion sums up.

abcb

hint: Does line 1 rhyme with line 2 or with line 3?
explanation: Lines 1 and 3 rhyme and lines 2 and 4 rhyme, so the scheme is **abab** in every stanza: heart/depart and care/air; earth/worth and needs/weeds; said/head and impart/heart; way/say and cheer/dear; chest/test and feast/least; show/grow and root/fruit. Some are near rhymes (earth/worth), but the pattern stays the same.

prompt: Match each line from *Words* with the poetic device it uses.

image.alt: A scroll showing a bird, a traveller with a staff, a dish of food and a looping arrow

left.text: But words, like summer birds, depart
The heart, a pilgrim upon earth
If words could satisfy the chest, / The world might hold a feast
'If words could satisfy…' opening both stanza 1 and stanza 5

hint: Look for 'like'; then for a direct comparison; then for exaggeration.
explanation: '**Like** summer birds' is a **simile** (comparison using *like*). 'The heart, **a pilgrim**' is a **metaphor**: the heart is called a pilgrim on a journey. 'The **world** might hold a **feast**' exaggerates hugely, so it is the **hyperbole** the book points out. Using 'If words could satisfy…' again in stanza 5 is **repetition**, which stresses the idea that words fail to satisfy. No line imitates a sound, so onomatopoeia is not used.

prompt: Put these ideas in the same order as the stanzas of *Words*.

items.text: A few true words give deeper joy than hosts of words.
Words fly away like summer birds, leaving empty air.
Words are like showy plants that bear no fruit.

prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: Birds flying away from a branch into the open sky

assertion: In the first stanza, the poet compares words to summer birds.
reason: Like summer birds that fly away, words often disappear and leave nothing behind but empty air.
hint: What do summer birds do when the season ends?
explanation: Both are true and R explains A. Summer birds visit for a short time and then **depart**, leaving 'but **empty air**'. Words are similar: they sound pleasant for a moment and then vanish without satisfying the heart. The comparison uses *like*, so it is a **simile**.

prompt: In *Weigh Your Words* by E. F. Hayward, what do these lines mean: *“We never can erase one thing, / We've written on a heart.”*?

image.alt: A balance scale weighing speech bubbles

options.text: We should always write letters in pencil so we can rub them out.
Words written in a diary can never be lost.
Hurtful words leave a lasting mark on a person's feelings that cannot be undone.
It is easy to make someone forget what we said.

hint: The stanza talks about the 'pain and sting' an idle word may start.
explanation: The poet uses a **metaphor**: our words are 'written' on someone's heart and cannot be erased. An **idle** (careless) word may cause pain and sting that lasts. So we should **'weigh' our words**, saying only what we mean; we would talk less, but our words would 'mean a whole lot more'.

prompt: In the past, people sent short messages such as greetings and condolences by **telegram**. Why did a telegram message have to be precise?

image.alt: A telegram form with word boxes, a stack of coins and a tapping telegraph key

options.text: Its price depended on the number of words sent.
It could be sent only at night.

Telegrams were read aloud on the radio.

hint: Think about what each extra word cost.
explanation: A telegram was a fast mode of communication whose **pricing was based on the number of words** transmitted, so senders kept messages short and **precise**. This links to the poem's idea that a few well-chosen words can mean more than many, which is also the message of 'Weigh Your Words'.
